questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+8y=12{e}^{-2x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $12{e}^{-2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-2$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha {e}^{-2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{-2x}+4(-2\alpha {e}^{-2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{-2x}) & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ (4-8+8)\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{e}^{-2x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12y=21{e}^{3x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+7\lambda +12 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =-4$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $21{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=3\alpha {e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=9\alpha {e}^{3x}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p}$, ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}9\alpha {e}^{3x}+7(3\alpha {e}^{3x})+12(\alpha {e}^{3x}) & =21{e}^{3x} \\ (9+21+12)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =21{e}^{3x} \\ 42\alpha  & =21 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=10{e}^{-x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{4x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{4x},$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =-1$ and $\lambda =4.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-x}.
$$

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}-3(\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x})-4(\alpha x{e}^{-x}) & =10{e}^{-x} \\ (x-2-3+3x-4x)\alpha {e}^{-x} & =10{e}^{-x} \\ -5\alpha {e}^{-x} & =10{e}^{-x} \\ -5\alpha  & =10 \\ \alpha  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2x{e}^{-x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=6{e}^{3x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =2$ or $\lambda =3$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{3x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p}$, ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}-5(\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x})+6(\alpha x{e}^{3x}) & =6{e}^{3x} \\ (9x+6-5-15x+6x)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =6{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha {e}^{3x} & =6{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=6x{e}^{3x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{3x}+6x{e}^{3x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-8\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+16y=6{e}^{4x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-8\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+16y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =4$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{4x}+Bx{e}^{4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{4x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $4$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =\alpha (2x+4{x}^{2}){e}^{4x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (2+16x+16{x}^{2}){e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (2+16x+16{x}^{2}){e}^{4x}-8\alpha (2x+4{x}^{2}){e}^{4x}+16\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ \alpha (2+16x+16{x}^{2}-16x-32{x}^{2}+16{x}^{2}){e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ 2\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{4x}+Bx{e}^{4x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}.
$$

Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-10\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+25y=8{e}^{5x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-10\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+25y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =5$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{5x}+Bx{e}^{5x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $8{e}^{5x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $5$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{5x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =\alpha (2x+5{x}^{2}){e}^{5x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (2+20x+25{x}^{2}){e}^{5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (2+20x+25{x}^{2}){e}^{5x}-10\alpha (2x+5{x}^{2}){e}^{5x}+25\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{5x} & =8{e}^{5x} \\ \alpha (2+20x+25{x}^{2}-20x-50{x}^{2}+25{x}^{2}){e}^{5x} & =8{e}^{5x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{5x} & =8{e}^{5x} \\ 2\alpha  & =8 \\ \alpha  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{5x}+Bx{e}^{5x}+4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x}.
$$

First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8=0\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $20{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2,$ which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha {e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}-4(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =20{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha (4-8+8){e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =5\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=5{e}^{2x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+5{e}^{2x}.
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=2{e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{2x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+10{e}^{2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2P+2Q+10 & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-4$ and $Q=0.$

We substitute this into the general particular integral and find that the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+0)+5{e}^{2x} \\  & =-4{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+5{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y={e}^{3x}
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x}+{e}^{3x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y={e}^{3x},\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{2(0)}+B(0){e}^{2(0)}+{e}^{3(0)} \\ 1 & =A+1 \\ A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=2A{e}^{2x}+2Bx{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{2x}+3{e}^{3x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the derivative we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2A{e}^{2(0)}+2B(0){e}^{2(0)}+B{e}^{2(0)}+3{e}^{3(0)} \\ 2 & =2A+B+3 \\ -1 & =2A+B \\ -1 & =2(0)+B \\ B & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=0$ and $B=-1,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y=-x{e}^{2x}+{e}^{3x}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} - 2y = 20 e ^ {3x}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. Since the roots of the characteristic equation are $\lambda = 1, -2,$ we get

$$
y_c  = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2 x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $20e^{3x},$ and $e^{3x}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha e^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 \alpha e ^{3x},
\quad \frac{\textrm{d}^2y_p}{\textrm{d}x^2} = 9  \alpha e ^{3x}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$  we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}9\alpha {e}^{3x}+3\alpha {e}^{3x}-2\alpha {e}^{3x} & =20{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha (9+3-2){e}^{3x} & =20{e}^{3x} \\ 10\alpha {e}^{3x} & =20{e}^{3x} \\ 10\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is 

$$
y_p = 2e^{3x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-2x}+2{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing and Repeated Roots
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. Since the characteristic equation has a single repeated root $\lambda = 3,$ the complementary solution is

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^{3x} + Bxe^{3x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $e^{3x},$ and $e^{3x}$ and $xe^{3x}$ are both terms in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha x^2e ^ {3x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(3{x}^{2}+2x)\alpha {e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=(9{x}^{2}+12x+2)\alpha {e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $y_p$, $y'_p$ and $y_p''$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{x}^{2}+12x+2)\alpha {e}^{3x}-6(3{x}^{2}+2x)\alpha {e}^{3x}+9\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ (9{x}^{2}+12x+2-18{x}^{2}-12x+9{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ 2\alpha  & =1 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(x) = \dfrac 1 2x^2 e ^{3x},
$$

and the general solution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{3x}+Bx{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving an Initial Value Problem
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}
$$

has the general solution

$$
Ae^{3 x} + Bxe^{3 x} + \dfrac 1 2 x ^2 e^{3 x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}, \qquad y(0) = 2 , \ \ y'(0) = 1.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{0}+B(0){e}^{0}+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}{e}^{0} \\ 2 & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=3A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{3x}+3Bx{e}^{3x}+x{e}^{3x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y'(0)=1$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3A{e}^{0}+B{e}^{0}+3B(0){e}^{0}+0{e}^{0}+\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}{e}^{0} \\ 1 & =3A+B \\ 1 & =3(2)+B \\ -5 & =B.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=2$ and $B=-5,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2{e}^{3x}-5x{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation takes the form

$$
a(x)y'' + b(x)y' + c(x) y = f(x)
$$

where $a(x),$ $b(x),$ and $c(x)$ are functions of $x$ only and $f(x)$ is a nonzero function.

In general, we say that a second-order ODE has **exponential forcing** if $f(x)$ is an exponential function. For example, the ODE below has exponential forcing:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 5\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 6y =10 e ^ {2x}
$$

The method for solving a second-order ODE with exponential forcing is similar to the method for solving a second-order ODE with polynomial forcing. The general solution is still the sum of the complementary solution $y_c$ (i.e., the solution to the associated homogeneous ODE) and a particular solution $y_p\mathbin{:}$

$$
y = y_c + y_p
$$

The only difference is in how we find a particular solution. Given a second-order ODE with exponential forcing $f(x) = ae^{bx},$ provided that $e^{bx}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, we assume that a particular solution takes the form

$$
y_p = \alpha e^{bx}
$$

where $b$ is a known constant and $\alpha$ is an unknown constant to be determined.

tutorials.name: Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing
tutorials.problem:
Let's solve the following second-order ODE with exponential forcing:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 5\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 6y =10 e ^ {2x}
$$

First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. The characteristic equation (or auxiliary equation) is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +2) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = -3$ or $\lambda = -2.$ Consequently, the complementary solution is

$$
y_c = Ae^{-2x} + Be^{-3x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $10e^{2x},$ and $e^{2x}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha e^{2x}
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} = 2 \alpha e ^{2x},
\quad \frac{\textrm{d}^2y_p}{\textrm{d}x^2} = 4  \alpha e ^{2x}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}+5(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+6\alpha {e}^{2x} & =10{e}^{2x} \\ 20\alpha {e}^{2x} & =10{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p = \dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}
$$

and the general solution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-3x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: The Case When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Linearly Dependent
tutorials.problem:
Given a second-order ODE with exponential forcing $f(x) = ae^{bx},$ if $e^{bx}$ *is* a term in the complementary solution, then $\alpha e^{bx}$ *cannot* be a particular solution. Instead, we assume that a particular solution takes the form

$$
y_p = \alpha x e^{bx}
$$

For example, let's find the solution to the following ODE:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 5\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 6y =3 e ^ {-2x}
$$

First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +3) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = -2$ or $\lambda = - 3.$ Consequently, the complimentary solution is

$$
y_c  = Ae^{-2x} + Be^{-3x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution to the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $3e^{-2x},$ and $e^{-2x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha x e^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-2\alpha x{e}^{-2x}+\alpha {e}^{-2x}, \\ \,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =4\alpha x{e}^{-2x}-2\alpha {e}^{-2x}-2\alpha {e}^{-2x} \\  & =4\alpha x{e}^{-2x}-4\alpha {e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$  we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{4\alpha x{e}^{-2x}}_{―}-4\alpha {e}^{-2x}+5({-2\alpha x{e}^{-2x}}_{―}+\alpha {e}^{-2x})+{6\alpha x{e}^{-2x}}_{―} & =3{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Canceling the underlined terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =3{e}^{-2x} \\ \alpha  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p = 3 x e^{-2x},
$$

and the general solution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-3x}+3x{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Second-Order ODEs With Exponential Forcing and Repeated Roots
tutorials.problem:
Given a second-order ODE with exponential forcing $f(x) = ae^{bx},$ if $e^{bx}$ and $xe^{bx}$ are *both* terms in the complementary solution, then neither can be a particular solution. Instead, we assume that a particular solution takes the form

$$
y_p = \alpha x^2 e^{bx}.
$$

For example, let's find the solution to the following ODE:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 12\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 36y = e ^{6x}
$$

First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)(\lambda -6) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = 6$ is a repeated root. Consequently, the complementary solution is

$$
y = Ae^{6 x} + Bxe^{6 x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $e^{6x},$ and $e^{6x}$ and $xe^{6x}$ are both terms in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha x^2 e^{6x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =6\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{6x}+2\alpha x{e}^{6x} \\ \,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =12x\alpha {e}^{6x}+36\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{6x}+2\alpha {e}^{6x}+12\alpha x{e}^{6x} \\  & =36\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{6x}+2\alpha {e}^{6x}+24\alpha x{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$  we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\underline {36 \alpha x^2 e ^{6x}}
+2 \alpha e ^{6x} +\underline{ 24 \alpha x e ^{6x} }-12(\underline{6 \alpha x^ 2e ^{6x} }+ 
\underline {2 \alpha x e^{6x}})
+\underline{36  \alpha x^2 e ^{6x}} = e^{6x}.
$$

Canceling the underlined terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\alpha {e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x}\,⇒\,\alpha =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p = \dfrac{1}{2} x^2 e^{6x},
$$

and the general solution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{c} \\  & =A{e}^{6x}+Bx{e}^{6x}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$
